summary: Describes the routing architecture of the NSFNET, centered on the new NSFNET Backbone. It focuses on the interface between the backbone and the networks attached to it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1093 describes how the NSFNET Backbone exchanged routing information with regional and peer networks. It explains the use of separate interior and exterior routing protocols and the policies that controlled which routes could be announced.

subtitle: How the NSFNET Backbone exchanged routing information with attached networks.

tldr.problem: The NSFNET Backbone needed a routing arrangement for its core and for regional and peer networks attached to it. Routing information had to be exchanged without creating inconsistent routes or loops.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a shortest-path-first interior routing protocol in the backbone and Exterior Gateway Protocol at network boundaries, with filters and Autonomous System checks controlling route exchange.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1093 records an informational description of the NSFNET routing architecture in February 1989, including requirements for attached gateways and an example configuration for gated.

sections.title: The NSFNET Routing Structure
sections.content:
The NSFNET Backbone formed the core of the NSFNET and connected regional backbones and peer networks such as the ARPANET and NASA Science Network. Inside the backbone, an interior routing protocol based on Shortest Path First (SPF) and adapted from IS-IS distributed routing information among backbone nodes.

At the boundaries, the backbone used the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) to exchange routing information with attached networks. Filtering based on routing policy databases was used to maintain consistency between the EGP and interior routing information.
sections.plainLanguage: The backbone used one routing method within its core and another to exchange routes with attached networks. Filters controlled which outside routes entered or left the backbone.

sections.title: Route Exchange and Metrics
sections.content:
Backbone nodes flooded address information through the core and ran the SPF algorithm to build routing tables. At the edges, the backbone and regional networks exchanged network reachability using EGP in interior mode. The architecture aimed for consistent information about reachable networks while controlling redistribution by Autonomous System number.

The backbone assigned its own metrics rather than trusting metrics received from regional networks. EGP announcements from the backbone to regional networks used a fixed metric of 128. The RFC also states that routes learned from one external interface must not be sent back through that same interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Backbone nodes calculated their routes from information shared inside the core. Boundary rules checked where external routes came from and limited how they were passed on.

sections.title: Rules for Regional Gateways
sections.content:
Each regional backbone needed a unique Autonomous System number. The backbone checked incoming announcements against both the network number and Autonomous System number; announcements from an unauthorized system were not trusted and could trigger an alarm to the Network Operations Center.

Regional gateways were expected to announce networks belonging to their own Autonomous System and to avoid redistributing routes learned through EGP back over that same route. The RFC recommends route filtering and says internal routing information should be able to override external routes. Regional networks could choose whether to generate a default route internally when their EGP connection to the backbone was working.
sections.plainLanguage: A regional gateway had to identify its Autonomous System and announce only routes allowed by the policy. These rules helped prevent route loops and unauthorized route announcements.

sections.title: Gateway Capabilities and Example Configuration
sections.content:
The RFC lists capabilities needed by attached gateways, including bidirectional exchange between interior and exterior routing, configurable metrics, route filtering, and the ability to prefer an internal route over an EGP route. Gateways should also allow administrators to control whether an EGP connection leads to a default route announcement.

An appendix gives extensions for the gated EGP implementation as an example. The RFC explicitly says these extensions were still in the design stage and could change; the example is not presented as a final protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways need configurable controls for route exchange and filtering. The appendix illustrates those controls for one implementation and says the example could change.
